Hi team, 

Firstly thanks for the updated vignettes posted at https://examples.distancesampling.org/, I find these worked examples extremely useful to go from a theoretical description in a paper to the practical steps of an analysis.

So far I have used (thanks in large part to your support!) several variations of distance sampling, most recently cue counts for gibbons. We're now looking at methods for estimating density and abundance with camera traps for some low density species, specifically the approach described in Howe et al. 2018 (attached for those who are not familiar). The paper excellent, with a clear description of the method, and the data is also published which is great.

I was wondering if there were any plans to produce vignettes or training courses on this new method, or if a R Markdown file for the duiker analysis described in Howe et al was available?

Cheers,

Olly

Scott

Good to hear from you; I remember you from a training workshop here in St Andrews 4 or 5 years ago.

There are two components to your question:
  • how is effort recorded, in the case of Howe's work, effort is the number of snapshot moments recorded by the camera divided by the recycle time of the shutter.  As they say in their paper:
    • We predetermine a ﬁnite set of snapshot moments within T _k , t units of time apart, at which an image of an animal could be obtained. Temporal eﬀort at the point is then T _k /t.
  • The second component is the proportion of the surrounding habitat over which the camera can detect animals.  This is the quantity theta/(2 x pi) described in the paper.  Assuming this quantity is the same for all cameras, the quantity theta/(2 x pi) can be entered as a multiplier (in Distance for Windows) or the argument sampling_fraction when working in R.
Hope that helps.

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling with camera traps - vignettes or training courses?
parts:
Scott, you can’t treat camera trap data like normal point transect data because of animal movement.  If you leave a camera at the point for a long time, eventually, animals will come close enough to be detected.  But if you take ‘snapshots’ at fixed periods of time, then that eliminates the bias from animal movement.  Each snapshot corresponds to a visit to the point in conventional point transect sampling.  So effort is number of snapshots – multiplied by the fraction of the circle covered by the camera’s sensor.  If snapshots are defined independently of animals, then you can choose the time between snapshots to be anything you want.  Non-independence becomes more of an issue the shorter you make the time between snapshots, so you need analysis methods that are robust to non-independence.  If the camera is triggered by animal movement, then more care is needed in choosing time between snapshots.  If you make this time large, you will overestimate abundance, because your snapshot sequences will always start with an animal present.  So the time needs to be such that animals will not normally pass through the sector covered by the sensor in a shorter time than the one you select.  For many animals, something of the order of 1-5 seconds might work OK.  If you take say 2 seconds, then you have to include in your effort the time the camera is operating divided by 2 seconds – in other words, you’ll have a ‘snapshot’ every 2 seconds, whether or not an animal has triggered the sensor, and choosing a short time ensures that any bias caused by having a snapshot whenever the sensor is triggered ensures any bias will be very small.

 

I hope that clarifies.

 

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Distance sampling with camera traps - vignettes or training courses?
parts:
Good day Scott, and thanks Eric and Steve,

Scott, regarding your question: "How are the snapshot moments defined/quantified": You define them as specific times of day. You also chose a daily time interval or intervals during which you will measure distances if animals are detected. 

It's helpful to plot detection times over the 24-hour day before measuring distances, because you might decide to reduce your daily survey duration to e.g. near dawn and dusk for crepuscular species or daylight hours for diurnal species (as in our article), and there's no need to measure distances to animals detected outside of this interval.

Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). If t = 3, you could define moments as e.g. 0, 3, 6..., 57 seconds after the even minute, OR as 2, 5, 8,..., etc. seconds after the even minute, in real time. Moments are the same for all cameras. Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments. 

Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..

Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.

Hope this helps,
Eric H

Good day Scott,
Re: activity period. Rowcliffe et al 2014 described methods for estimating the proportion of time active at camera height (and so available for detection by CTs), directly from times of detection, within any time interval (e.g. 24, 12, or 8 hours). There's an R package 'activity'. This can help you select daily Tk, and also account for temporally limited availability for detection within Tk.

Selection of t is a trade-off between missed observations of e.g. fast-moving animals close to the camera (missed if t is too large - no bias but costs you data), and data management (at some point, more observations of the same animals at almost the same location just creates more work measuring distances, without improving precision). Also, with smaller t, trigger speed and unavoidable delays between recordings could start to cause slight bias. Optimal values haven't been identified, and would likely vary across species and camera placements.

Eric H

It's helpful to plot detection times over the 24-hour day before measuring distances, because you might decide to reduce your daily survey duration to e.g. near dawn and dusk for crepuscular species or daylight hours for diurnal species (as in our article), and there's no need to measure distances to animals detected outside of this interval.
 
Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). If t = 3, you could define moments as e.g. 0, 3, 6..., 57 seconds after the even minute, OR as 2, 5, 8,..., etc. seconds after the even minute, in real time. Moments are the same for all cameras. Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments. 
 
Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..
 
Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.
 
Hope this helps,
Eric H

Good day Scott,

As Eric and Steve mention, we accept and include non-independent observations. If its midpoint is visible, and the time is within Tk and during a snapshot moment, we record distance and include the observations. It doesn't cause cause bias because a single animal can only be detected once per location per snapshot moment. 

The issue with apparent heaping is potentially more complicated. Measuring distances to "resting" animals caused problems in simulations, because an animal that remains in front of the camera can contribute large numbers of observations, and if they are at moderate to far distances, decreasing functions may not fit the data well. Our (imperfect) solution was to avoid sampling during times when animals "rest". 

Animals that are awake and moving slightly (thus triggering the sensor) but not going anywhere could cause the same effect, and we don't have a clear reason to sensor the observations (the animal is "active").

I would suggest checking the times of day when cameras detected these lingering animals, and see if they are similar. If there are specific times of day when animals are at their most mobile (e.g. crepuscular?), such that animals detected at these times pass by the camera (often contributing > 1, but not dozens or hundreds, of observations) rather than lingering in front of it, then you could limit Tk to these times. That could exclude most or all lingering animals from the data, improving fit without causing bias. 
  
Bessone et al. (2020) sensored observations of animals obviously reacting to the camera, and this improved fit (another imperfect solution to a similar problem).   https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.13602. 

If you had only one animal that lingered in front of a camera and this animal created a "bump" in the observed distances far from 0, you could just say so and exclude the animal or most of the observations it contributed. 

Eric

If the burst settings were such that if any of images fell on one of the pre-defined intervals (e.g. :00, :02, :04 etc of each minute), then you would use each of those that fell on one of those intervals as a detection (snapshot) and measure distance.

This could occur if your camera sensor's recovery time is greater than the chosen CTDS interval period divided by the number of images per burst. In your case,  X second periods / 3 photos. If you are using the typical 2s period, then 2/3 = 0.67 seconds. If your camera trap sensor's recovery time during bursts is greater than 0.67, then it would be possible for 2 photos taken in a single 3-photo burst to be used as two independent snapshots. This is pretty slow for a modern camera trap, but if you took more photos per burst, you are more likely to overlap multiple snapshot moments (e.g. 10 image burst, t = 2s, then 2/10 = 0.2s which is a pretty quick recovery time).

Snapshot moments are independent of the trigger moment, if I understand correctly. This is why video is sometimes used - the sensor is triggered at 14:21:17, video recorded for 15 seconds, then snapshots at e.g. 14:21:18, 14:21:20, 14:21:22, and 14:21:24 are selected from that video, with the animal leaving the field of view at 14:21:25. In this example, you would have pre-defined your 't' interval to be 2s. With a photo based approach, you would set the camera to take enough images that one falls close to each of these pre-defined moments during the period the animal is in front of the sensor (ignoring resting/avoidance/curiosity for the moment for simplicity).

Please let me know if I'm mistaken here - I have yet to implement our survey but will be basing our design on the assumptions above! We intend to use photos rather than videos for data management and processing reasons.

Hi Scott,

According to the original article, snapshot moments should be independent of triggering times, and predetermined as specific times of day. E.g. 0, 2, 4, ...., 58 seconds after the even minute for and interval (t ) = 2 seconds. In practice, we might look at our data after they had been collected and decide to set the interval to 1 or 3 or more seconds (to avoid missed detections, or unnecessary work), but we would still measure distances at those specific moments... Also, we would often measure distances to an animal or animals multiple times as it or they pass through the field of view (whenever it/they moves slowly enough to be present in the field of view during > 1 snapshot moment). We recommended programming cameras to record either video or long, rapid, bursts of still images, to ensure that some images would align (almost) perfectly with snapshot moments.

I know there has been some discussion about how to collect data when cameras are not programmed to record e.g. video. With small t and cameras that can be triggered again immediately after recording an image, bias induced by the fact that observations of distance are not independent of trigger times should be slight. This approach would require small t  (not sure how small, but probably no longer than 2 seconds, and ideally shorter) so that observed distances would describe the animals' path through the zone of potential detection, not the location upon initial detection, which is expected to yield a positively biased distribution of observed distances. Multiple observations of distance to slow-moving animals would be recorded during a single pass through the zone of potential detection.

Regarding your specific question, I think whether or not your 3 images would be recorded as one or as 2 or 3 observations depends on what t has been set to, and how far apart in time those 3 images are in time. E.g. if t = 2 and the images are 1 second apart, we would measure distances to animals in the first and third image. If t = 1 and the images are 2 seconds apart, we would miss detections at half of our snapshot moments, causing severe negative bias. You would only treat 3 images as one observation of distance if the time elapsed between images was much less than t.

Eric H

Good day Scott,

As Eric and Steve mention, we accept and include non-independent observations. If its midpoint is visible, and the time is within Tk and during a snapshot moment, we record distance and include the observations. It doesn't cause cause bias because a single animal can only be detected once per location per snapshot moment. 

The issue with apparent heaping is potentially more complicated. Measuring distances to "resting" animals caused problems in simulations, because an animal that remains in front of the camera can contribute large numbers of observations, and if they are at moderate to far distances, decreasing functions may not fit the data well. Our (imperfect) solution was to avoid sampling during times when animals "rest". 

Animals that are awake and moving slightly (thus triggering the sensor) but not going anywhere could cause the same effect, and we don't have a clear reason to sensor the observations (the animal is "active").

I would suggest checking the times of day when cameras detected these lingering animals, and see if they are similar. If there are specific times of day when animals are at their most mobile (e.g. crepuscular?), such that animals detected at these times pass by the camera (often contributing > 1, but not dozens or hundreds, of observations) rather than lingering in front of it, then you could limit Tk to these times. That could exclude most or all lingering animals from the data, improving fit without causing bias. 
  
Bessone et al. (2020) sensored observations of animals obviously reacting to the camera, and this improved fit (another imperfect solution to a similar problem).   https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2664.13602. 

If you had only one animal that lingered in front of a camera and this animal created a "bump" in the observed distances far from 0, you could just say so and exclude the animal or most of the observations it contributed.

Re: activity period. Rowcliffe et al 2014 described methods for estimating the proportion of time active at camera height (and so available for detection by CTs), directly from times of detection, within any time interval (e.g. 24, 12, or 8 hours). On Tuesday, June 9, 2020 at 2:36:42 AM UTC+10, Eric Howe wrote:

Good day Scott, and thanks Eric and Steve,

 
Scott, regarding your question: "How are the snapshot moments defined/quantified": You define them as specific times of day. You also chose a daily time interval or intervals during which you will measure distances if animals are detected. 
 
It's helpful to plot detection times over the 24-hour day before measuring distances, because you might decide to reduce your daily survey duration to e.g. near dawn and dusk for crepuscular species or daylight hours for diurnal species (as in our article), and there's no need to measure distances to animals detected outside of this interval.
 
Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). If t = 3, you could define moments as e.g. 0, 3, 6..., 57 seconds after the even minute, OR as 2, 5, 8,..., etc. seconds after the even minute, in real time. Moments are the same for all cameras. Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments. 
 
Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..
 
Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.
 
Hope this helps,
Eric H

parts: Here's a little graphic I made to help illustrate the method to our team, perhaps it would be useful. Here, we pre-selected a t of 2 seconds, and with the snapshot falling on :00, :02, :04  etc of every minute. This shows the images or frames we would select under 4 different setups - one video, and 3 photo mode setups with different recovery times and burst modes (depending on camera model). Here, an animal enters the sensor FOV at 08:01:12.8 and remains in view for about 12 seconds. Each sensor triggers, and following a short delay (trigger time, dotted orange) begins to capture video or bursts of images. From this data, we select either video frames or photos (red lines) that are closest to the snapshot time (blue lines). For the video mode, a continuous video is captured for a defined length of time. For the photo modes, images are recorded with each firing of the sensor. This  shows why a short recovery time (between bursts) is required for CTDS. If the recovery time (a.k.a interval) was set to 15 seconds, the sensor would only fire once during the animal's time in the FOV. By setting the interval low, or using a higher number of images in each burst, a more continuous coverage of images is captured, allowing you to select images that are closest to the snapshot moments, and reducing bias. You can also see here how a single trigger event can produce more than one capture, if the burst continues over two snapshot moments (or includes images that are the closest to two snapshot moments, even if they don't fully overlap).

Additionally, in case it helps: Because the zone of potential detection is a sector, not a circle, randomizing sampling locations is insufficient to avoid bias in observed distances upon initial detection. Animals approaching the camera from in front of it contribute observations near the maximum range of the sensor, and observations closer to the camera, where detection probability as a function of distance is actually high, are missed. When animals approach from behind, we detect them at short distances (as expected), and miss them at longer distances, but we expect more misses at long distances with decreasing effectiveness of the sensor, so, on average, the bias in observed distances is positive. Figure 3.1 of my thesis https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/bitstream/handle/10023/18859/EricHowePhDThesis.pdf?sequence=3 (p 69 of the thesis, p 86 of the pdf document) attempts to illustrate the bias in distances observed upon initial detection.  

We avoid the bias by recording distance observations at multiple points along the animals' path through the zone of potential detection (small t), so those observations at short distances aren't missed. 

For comparison, Rowcliffe et al.'s (2008) Random Encounter Model accounted for the sector-shaped area sampled by "averaging across all possible angles of approach" (see their Figure 1), so they didn't ignore this potential source of bias, they just dealt with it differently.

Eric H

Good day Scott, and thanks Eric and Steve,

 

 

Scott, regarding your question: "How are the snapshot moments defined/quantified": You define them as specific times of day. You also chose a daily time interval or intervals during which you will measure distances if animals are detected. 

 

It's helpful to plot detection times over the 24-hour day before measuring distances, because you might decide to reduce your daily survey duration to e.g. near dawn and dusk for crepuscular species or daylight hours for diurnal species (as in our article), and there's no need to measure distances to animals detected outside of this interval.

 

Also choose a value for t (duration of time step between snapshot moments). If t = 3, you could define moments as e.g. 0, 3, 6..., 57 seconds after the even minute, OR as 2, 5, 8,..., etc. seconds after the even minute, in real time. Moments are the same for all cameras. Regardless of when a camera is triggered, distances are measured only at these moments. 

 

Tk is the total number of seconds a camera operates at location k. It's convenient to define a daily Tk, in seconds. This is the "time interval during which you will measure distances" above, so it might be less than the number of seconds in 24 hours; it might be the number of seconds within a 2- or 12-hour period. Multiply this by the number of days a camera operated and could have detected animals at a location to obtain Tk at that location. Then, dividing Tk by t (both in seconds) gives you the total number of opportunities to detect an animal at a location over the duration of a survey. This is your temporal effort at that location. Enter it as "Effort" in software IFF you are quantifying spatial effort < than a circle using a multiplier or the sampling_fraction argument. Alternatively, you can avoid multipliers and calculate Effort as described in the article (incorporating both spatial and temporal components)..

 

Note that if we detected one animal at every opportunity, the encounter rate would be 1.0. In practice, encounter rates (detections per opportunity) are very low with camera trap point transects, because we observe no animals during most opportunities.

 

Hope this helps,

Eric H
